options: An attribute's value is fixed when the row is first loaded and is never updated afterward, no matter what the source system says
The dimension has zero attributes
The dimension is deleted and reloaded every night
The attribute is updated every time the source changes, with no history kept
questions.explain: Type 0 attributes are deliberately frozen at insert time — the ETL process never writes an UPDATE against that column again, even if the source value later changes.

questions.q: Which of these is a realistic real-world example of an SCD Type 0 attribute?
options: A customer's DateFirstPurchase column
A customer's current phone number
A product's current list price
A salesperson's current sales region assignment
questions.explain: The date of a customer's very first purchase, by definition, doesn't change when later orders happen — it's a fixed historical fact, a classic Type 0 attribute.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say Type 0 needs to be an explicit, documented rule rather than just "we never got around to writing an UPDATE for this column"?
options: A future ETL change (like a generic "refresh all attributes" step) could silently overwrite the value with no error and no one noticing
SQL Server physically prevents UPDATE statements from targeting date columns
Undocumented columns are automatically deleted by the database engine
It has no real risk — the distinction doesn't matter in practice
questions.explain: Without an explicit write-once rule, a later change to the ETL pipeline can quietly overwrite a value that was supposed to be permanent, with no warning.

questions.q: What's the key difference between SCD Type 0 and SCD Type 1?
options: Type 0 deliberately refuses to update the value even when the source changes; Type 1 deliberately allows the value to be overwritten when the source changes
Type 0 keeps full history in new rows; Type 1 does not
Type 0 only applies to numeric columns; Type 1 only applies to text columns
There is no real difference between the two
questions.explain: Both end up with one row and no history, but the intent differs: Type 1 is designed to accept overwrites, while Type 0 is designed to reject them entirely.

questions.q: According to the lesson, does Microsoft's own Fabric data warehouse documentation give SCD Type 0 its own named heading alongside Types 1, 2, and 3?
options: No — Type 0 is a term from Kimball's dimensional modeling vocabulary that describes the absence of change-handling, not a documented Microsoft pattern
Yes — Type 0 is Microsoft's recommended default for every dimension attribute
Yes, but only for date dimensions
No — Microsoft's documentation doesn't cover any SCD types at all
questions.explain: Microsoft's guidance names Types 1, 2, and 3 as the common SCD types; Type 0 isn't a change-handling technique so much as the deliberate absence of one, applied to a specific column.
